title: Year three opens: after Moses
hookLine: the Prophets are the second part of the Tanakh; they begin the day Moses dies
carry: the story goes on without moses
last: THE TORAH, THE PRAYER, THE YEAR.

lines: WHO IS GONE, WHO IS LEFT.
cards: After the death of Moses. Those are the first words of the next book. Not a fresh start: a death, right at the top of the page.

Most books start by introducing someone. This one starts by saying who is gone, and only then turns to the man left standing: Joshua son of Nun, who had served Moses. One sentence holds the old leader and the new one.
The Torah has an ending. The people's story doesn't. This year, it walks on into the second part of the Bible.

teach.b: Jews call their Bible the Tanakh, a name built from the first letters of its three parts: Torah, the teaching; Nevi'im, the Prophets; Ketuvim, the Writings. Years one and two read the first part. Now, the second.
Nevi'im is the plural of navi, prophet. The first surprise is what's in it.

teach.h: IT OPENS WITH HISTORY: THE FORMER PROPHETS.
teach.b: Before the prophets who speak in poetry, Nevi'im opens with books that read like history: Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings. Jewish tradition calls them the Former Prophets. So why call history prophecy?
The Torah gives a clue. When Moses protests that he can't speak well enough to face Pharaoh, God answers: "Aaron thy brother shall be thy prophet."
There, a navi is a spokesman, the one who carries words from one person to another. A prophet isn't mainly a fortune teller, but someone a message travels through.
These books carry their message through what happens: when the people keep faith, when they don't, and what follows. The second surprise is how it starts.
"Moses My servant is dead." That's God, speaking to Joshua, in the book's second verse. No long scene of grief; the Torah already gave the mourning its days.
A plain sentence, then straight on: arise, cross this Jordan.
The teacher of the whole Torah is gone, and the story goes on with someone new, in a harder place. That's the shape of the year ahead: a people, after Moses, working it out.

how: In synagogues, each Shabbat Torah reading is followed by a haftarah, a passage from the Prophets; on Simchat Torah, as the Torah ends with Moses' death, the haftarah is commonly the opening of the book of Joshua.

games.q: you're Joshua. Moses, who led the people through the whole Torah, has died. God speaks to you for the first time in your new role. what comes next?
o: more time to mourn before anything else.
an order to cross the Jordan now.
a promise that another Moses will come.
games.why: "Moses My servant is dead," and straight on: arise, cross this Jordan. the mourning already happened in Deuteronomy. the story doesn't wait.

practice: If there's a Bible near you, Joshua's first verse is on the first page after Deuteronomy; if not, hear it in plain words: after the death of Moses, the servant of the Lord, the Lord spoke to Joshua son of Nun, who had served Moses.
Keep only four words, after the death of, and let them bring to mind someone whose work you now carry on, a parent, a teacher, a friend. Stay with them a while, and with what they handed you.
